# The six verbs

Six words do most of the work anyone does to a table. You can keep rows,
choose columns, add a column, summarize by group, sort, and take the first
few. Almost everything else people do is an arrangement of those six.

The claim is older than any tool you have used. In 1970, E. F. Codd showed
that questions about tables need only a handful of operations, each taking a
table and giving a table back, so that the operations compose without limit
[@codd1970]. SQL gave that algebra an English surface four years later
[@chamberlin1974], and every tool since has carried the same handful under
different names: dplyr, pandas, polars, Spark. The six verbs in this part are
those survivors, spelled once. Nothing here is god's invention, and that is
the point. You have already met every idea in this part, in at least one
other spelling.

The part runs in one direction. The first chapter shows a whole pipeline, so
you know what the pieces are for before you meet them one at a time. Six
short chapters then take one verb each, a seventh adds renaming and dropping
repeats, and an eighth gathers the small words (`by`, `as`, `where`,
`all_but`, `descending`) that travel between verbs. Two practice chapters
close the part: one where you read pipelines, and one where you write them.

One law holds the part together: **one word, one meaning**. `by` means the
same thing after `summarize` as it does after `take`; `as` always names what
was made; nothing is spelled two ways. The same law is applied to this book's
own structure. Every verb chapter is built one way, and you can hold it to
the shape. It opens with a question about data, and the verb arrives as the
answer. The first pipeline is followed by the same sentence in the grammar's
own words, in italics; read that one aloud, and every later pipeline reads
the same way. The middle of a chapter shows what the verb can vary and argues
one design decision. Two sections close every verb chapter, always last,
always under the same names: *What travels with it* lists the small words the
verb shares with the rest of the grammar, and *What it refuses* shows the
refusals live, in both languages. The sameness is deliberate. A book whose
chapters share one shape is faster to learn the second time than the first.

The promise this part answers for is the preface's: read a pipeline aloud on
day one, write one on day two, and still have it after a year away. When the
practice chapters are behind you, the first two clauses are due. The third is
what the sameness is for.
